title: The Whale That Recognised Herself in a Mirror

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For half a century, one of the most debated tests in animal psychology has been the mirror test, an experiment in which a coloured mark is placed on an anaesthetised or distracted animal in a spot it cannot see directly, and researchers then watch whether the animal touches or investigates the mark once it catches sight of itself in a mirror. Only a short list of species has ever been reported to pass: a few great apes, Asian elephants, bottlenose dolphins, orcas, a species of cleaner fish and, remarkably, the Eurasian magpie. Whether the test measures genuine self-awareness or something narrower remains contested, but passing it is still treated as one of the clearest behavioural signs that an animal can distinguish its own reflection from that of another individual. A recent study set out to discover whether belugas, small white whales related to narwhals rather than to dolphins, belong on that list.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The research took place at the New York Aquarium, run by the Wildlife Conservation Society, and involved four belugas: three adult females named Kathy, Marina and Natasha, and a younger female called Maris, who was Natasha's own daughter. Between February and November 2001 the animals took part in 98 separate sessions split into two phases. In the first phase a large two-way mirror was lowered into one section of their pool on some days and, on other days, a transparent acrylic panel of identical size was used instead as a control, so that researchers could distinguish curiosity about a novel object from a specific response to a reflection. Across the study the whales spent roughly 27 hours in front of the mirror and about 23 hours in front of the plain panel.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: From the very first sessions, the whales treated the mirror differently from the control panel. They lingered near it, angled their bodies to bring particular areas into view, and produced a cluster of behaviours rarely seen elsewhere in their daily routine: blowing strings of bubbles while facing the glass, performing slow barrel rolls, stretching their necks, opening their mouths wide towards the surface and rotating a pectoral flipper as if to inspect it. These actions, described by the researchers as self-directed rather than social, appeared within the very first mirror session for two of the four animals, Natasha and Maris, after little more than two hours of exposure.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Having established that the whales attended to the mirror in an unusual way, the researchers moved to a second, more demanding phase: the classic mark test. A harmless cosmetic mark, five to eight centimetres across, was applied to a part of the body the whale could not see without a mirror, most often just behind an eye or an ear. On other occasions a sham procedure was carried out, in which the whale was touched in the same way but no visible mark was left, allowing the team to separate a reaction to being touched from a reaction to seeing a mark.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Natasha, the older of the two whales that had shown strong interest in the mirror, passed one of the three mark tests she was given. When a real mark had been applied, she oriented the marked patch of skin towards the mirror repeatedly, spending a total of three minutes and forty seconds doing so across fourteen separate approaches. When she carried an invisible sham mark instead, the equivalent behaviour lasted only twenty-three seconds across four approaches, a difference the researchers regarded as strong evidence that she was inspecting the mark itself rather than merely enjoying the mirror.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Maris, by contrast, produced an equally rich range of self-directed behaviours at the mirror but never showed any sign of orienting towards her own mark. The researchers were careful not to treat this as a failure so much as a reminder that, even among species that can pass the test, individual animals vary enormously in how, and how quickly, they respond, a pattern also documented in chimpanzees and dolphins. Both whales, notably, preferred to view the mirror with their right eye, a bias that hints at some degree of lateralised processing in how the brain handles this kind of visual information.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The result is significant because it extends a capacity long associated mainly with the dolphin family to a different lineage of toothed whales, the Monodontidae, which includes belugas and narwhals. Combined with earlier reports in elephants, magpies and even a species of cleaner wrasse no larger than a human finger, the beluga findings support the view that some form of mirror self-recognition has evolved independently, more than once, in animals with very different brains and very different lifestyles, rather than being a single trait inherited from a common ancestor.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The authors are cautious about overstating what the test proves. Passing it does not necessarily mean an animal possesses the same rich sense of self reported by humans, and the fact that only two of the four belugas tested responded strongly shows how easily such abilities can be missed if only a single individual, or a small sample, is studied. What the experiment does establish, they argue, is that belugas are capable of processing a mirror image as a reflection of their own body, a finding that adds one more branch, quite a distant one, to the small evolutionary tree of animals known to recognise themselves.
